title: The binding of Isaac (Genesis 22)
hookLine: the hardest story in Genesis; Jewish readers have argued over it for two thousand years

lines: THINE ONLY SON, WHOM THOU LOVEST.
cards: In the old JPS translation it begins: "God did prove Abraham." God calls his name, and Abraham answers with one Hebrew word, hineni: here I am.
Then the command, each phrase heavier: "Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." Take him to the land of Moriah, and offer him there on a mountain.
This is the son Sarah laughed about: the son of the promise, the stars, the whole future. Abraham gets up early, saddles his donkey, splits the wood, and walks for three days.
The Torah tells us nothing about what he feels. Jewish readers have argued over this story for a very long time; this lesson won't settle it.

teach.b: On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain alone, Isaac carrying the wood.
And Isaac speaks, the only time he does in this story: my father, he says, and then: "Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?"
Abraham answers: "God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son." And the Torah says: they went both of them together. Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac, and lifts the knife.
An angel calls: Abraham, Abraham. Hineni, again.

teach.h: LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.
teach.b: "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." He sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, and offers it instead.
Jews call this the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in the verse: Isaac was bound, not sacrificed. Here the tradition wrestles.

teach.h: DEVOTION, A NO, OR A SILENCE?
teach.b: Some read it as the peak of devotion, a man ready to give everything. It's read on Rosh Hashanah, and the Talmud connects the ram's horn, the shofar, to this ram.

teach.h: THEY WENT BOTH OF THEM TOGETHER.
teach.b: Others read the ending as the point: God stops the knife, and they hear the Torah saying no to child sacrifice. Others feel the silence.
The same Abraham who argued with God for the strangers of Sodom says nothing for his own son. The next chapter opens with Sarah's death, and a midrash says she died when she heard what had happened.
And when Abraham walks down the mountain, the verse mentions only him. Where is Isaac? The Torah doesn't say.
None of these readings cancels the others. The tradition keeps them all, and keeps asking.

how: Jews read the Akedah on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar, a ram's horn, recalls the ram; many prayer books also include it in the daily morning service.

games.q: you're Isaac, walking up the mountain carrying the wood. you see the fire and the knife, but no animal. what do you do?
o: ask your father where the lamb is.
games.why: he asks, "where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?" Abraham answers, God will provide, my son, and they go on together.

practice: Bring to mind one question you can't resolve, about this story or your own life: a loss that doesn't make sense, a choice you still can't judge.
Don't try to answer it; let it sit with you, the way the tradition lets this story sit, and breathe beside it. If you pray, you can bring the question into your prayer.
